newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH TO STRIKE AGAINST GOVT CUTS, UNEMPLOYMENT.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH TO STRIKE AGAINST GOVT CUTS, UNEMPLOYMENT.

text.p: French schools, hospitals, trains and airline flights will be hit by a strike on Thursday against government cutbacks and record unemployment in a first big test of labour unrest since the crippling strikes of late 1995.
Government offices and agencies face disruption or closure for the day and workers at the state-owned gas and electricity companies will also stop work, but power cuts are not expected.

Postal workers will join the action and a rail strike is expected to reduce services to one in three trains on main lines, although the SNCF state railway said the high-speed Channel Tunnel service between London and Paris should run normally.

The 24-hour strike is spearheaded by civil servants fighting government plans to trim their numbers by nearly 6,000 next year as part of a wider drive to get French finances in order to qualify for monetary union and a single European currency.
Teachers will bear the brunt of the austerity drive, with a loss of 2,300 permanent jobs and the layoff of some 15,000 short-term contract staff, seen as the thin end of the wedge.

The other main motive is frustration over record 12.6 percent unemployment, still rising with more than three million jobless despite President Jacques Chirac's May 1995 election pledge to make employment his top priority.

Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin backed the strikes on Wednesday, accusing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservative coalition of a "social and economic error which is dragging France into a tailspin".

While the CFDT, the largest trade union, and other labour leaders have yet to discuss plans beyond Thursday's strikes and demonstrations, the Communist-led CGT is already trying to muster support for follow-up action.

Labour Minister Jacques Barrot pleaded with civil servants to avoid any action that could damage the French economy -- clearly mindful of the public sector strikes which crippled France for 24 days last November and December.

"I cannot believe they do not feel, at the bottom of their hearts, their loyalty to the rest of the country," Barrot told reporters. He asked civil servants to "know just where to stop, when the French economy would hurt too much".
The seven main civil service unions have organised a march through central Paris on Thursday starting at the Place de la Republique.

Jospin urged Socialist party members to join the demonstrations which will be led by Nicole Notat, head of the CFDT, Marc Blondel vociferous government critic and head of the Force Ouvriere union, and CGT leader Louis Viannet.
A strike by air traffic controllers and staff at airlines Air France and Air Inter Europe is expected to cause serious disruption, mainly for medium-haul flights.
Air Inter alone will cut its total flights from 500 to 110, while a minimum air controllers' service will hit international flights and cause delays to flights through French airspace.
The railway strike starts at 1800 GMT on Wednesday and runs until 0600 GMT on Friday.

Doctors will also protest for 24 hours on Thursday. Private specialists who object to social security spending cuts plan to limit treatment to emergency cases. On the other side of the fence, general practitioners who support social security reform but feel it is losing direction also plan minimum services.
Limited disruption is expected on the Paris buses, Metro underground rail service and the suburban RER commuter lines due to a strike call limited to the CGT union.
The CGT also called on lighthouse keepers to put on a "sound and light show" on Thursday in defence of the public service.
